title: UVF kills Peter Ward on Malvern Street
summary: Gunmen from the re-formed Ulster Volunteer Force shoot three young Catholic barmen leaving a pub off the Shankill Road. Eighteen-year-old Peter Ward dies. The UVF had already killed two people that summer.
significance: Prime Minister Terence O'Neill bans the UVF. Loyalist fear that O'Neill's modest reforms will sell out Ulster is part of the backdrop to everything that follows.
questions: Who were the UVF?
Why did loyalists distrust Terence O'Neill?

title: Civil rights association founded
summary: The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) is formed. Its demands: one man, one vote in council elections; an end to gerrymandered boundaries; fair allocation of council housing; repeal of the Special Powers Act; and disbanding the B-Specials police reserve.
significance: Borrowing tactics from the US civil rights movement, NICRA framed Catholic grievances as rights within the UK, not a demand for a united Ireland.
questions: What was gerrymandering in Derry?
What were the B-Specials?

title: Caledon house squat
summary: Nationalist MP Austin Currie squats in a council house in Caledon that had been given to a 19-year-old single Protestant woman with unionist connections, while Catholic families with children waited.
significance: A small protest that made the housing grievance impossible to ignore, and pushed the civil rights campaign onto the streets.

title: First civil rights march
summary: A few thousand people march from Coalisland to Dungannon. Police stop them entering the town centre, where loyalists have gathered to counter-protest. The march ends peacefully with songs and speeches.
significance: The template for the marches that followed: peaceful protest, a loyalist counter-demonstration, and police siding with the counter-protest.

title: Police baton marchers in Derry
summary: A banned civil rights march in Derry's Waterside is trapped between two police lines and batoned. MPs are among the injured. An RTÉ cameraman films it, and the footage goes around the world.
significance: Often called the start of the Troubles. Television made Northern Ireland's problems an international story overnight.
questions: Why was the march banned?
Why do people say the Troubles began here?

title: Ambush at Burntollet Bridge
summary: Student group People's Democracy marches from Belfast to Derry, modelled on the 1965 Selma march. On the fourth day, at Burntollet Bridge, about 200 loyalists, some of them off-duty B-Specials, attack with clubs and stones while police largely stand by.
significance: Convinced many nationalists the state would not protect them. Rioting broke out in Derry that night.
questions: Who were People's Democracy?
Why did the march go to Derry?

title: Battle of the Bogside
summary: An Apprentice Boys parade passing the Bogside sparks clashes. For two days residents behind barricades fight the RUC with stones and petrol bombs. Police use CS gas for the first time in the UK. 'You are now entering Free Derry' is painted on a gable wall.
significance: The RUC was exhausted and riots spread to Belfast. London had to send in the Army.
questions: Who are the Apprentice Boys?
What was Free Derry?

title: British troops on the streets
summary: Soldiers march into Derry to relieve the police. It is the start of Operation Banner, which will last 38 years and become the British Army's longest continuous deployment.
significance: Many Catholics first welcomed the troops as protectors. That welcome lasted less than a year.
questions: Why were the troops welcomed at first?
What went wrong between the Army and Catholics?

title: Bombay Street burned
summary: In two nights of rioting in Belfast, loyalist crowds burn Catholic homes. Bombay Street, on the line between the Falls and the Shankill, is gutted. Around 1,800 families, most of them Catholic, flee their homes during August and September.
significance: The old IRA was mocked as 'I Ran Away' for failing to defend Catholic areas. The Army builds the first 'peace lines' in September.

title: Republicans split: the Provisionals
summary: At the Sinn Féin conference in Dublin, traditionalists walk out over a vote to end the boycott of parliaments. Together with the IRA split the month before, this creates the Provisional IRA and the Official IRA.
significance: The Provisionals, rooted in defending Belfast's Catholic streets, become the main republican force of the next 30 years.
questions: What's the difference between the Official and Provisional IRA?

title: Arms Crisis in Dublin
summary: Taoiseach Jack Lynch sacks ministers Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney over an alleged plan to import guns for northern nationalists. Charges against Blaney are dropped and Haughey is acquitted.
significance: Showed how close parts of the Irish state came to arming northern nationalists. Haughey later became Taoiseach.

title: Falls Curfew
summary: After an arms search turns into a riot, the Army seals off the Lower Falls for 36 hours and searches house to house. Four civilians are killed.
significance: Ended the honeymoon between Catholics and the Army. IRA recruitment surged.

title: First British soldier killed
summary: Gunner Robert Curtis is shot dead by the IRA during rioting in north Belfast, the first soldier killed on duty in the Troubles.
significance: Marks the Provisional IRA moving from defence to an offensive campaign against the Army.

title: Internment and Ballymurphy
summary: In dawn raids, soldiers arrest 342 men for detention without trial. All are nationalists or republicans; no loyalists are taken. In Ballymurphy over the next three days, soldiers shoot dead ten civilians. A 2021 inquest found all were innocent.
significance: Internment was a disaster. Violence rose sharply, and the Free Derry no-go area went back up behind barricades.
questions: Why was internment one-sided?
What happened in Ballymurphy?

title: McGurk's Bar bombing
summary: A UVF bomb destroys a Catholic-owned bar, killing 15 people. Police and Army sources falsely suggested it was an IRA bomb that went off by accident.
significance: The deadliest attack in Belfast during the Troubles. The false 'own goal' story fed nationalist distrust of the authorities for decades.

title: Bloody Sunday
summary: Paratroopers open fire on a civil rights march against internment. Thirteen men are killed on the day and another dies later. The 2010 Saville Inquiry found none of them posed any threat. David Cameron apologised in the Commons.
significance: Perhaps the single most damaging day for the British state in Ireland. Young people queued to join the IRA, and 1972 became the deadliest year of the Troubles.
questions: What did the Widgery and Saville inquiries find?
Why does Bloody Sunday matter so much?

title: British Embassy burned in Dublin
summary: On a national day of mourning for the Bloody Sunday dead, a crowd of tens of thousands surrounds the British Embassy and burns it out.
significance: The high point of anger in the Republic, and a low point in relations between Dublin and London.
wiki: Burning of the British Embassy in Dublin

title: Stormont suspended: direct rule
summary: London suspends the Northern Ireland parliament after 50 years of unionist government and rules directly through a Secretary of State, William Whitelaw.
significance: The end of unionist self-government. Every peace plan from here on tries to bring back devolved government that both communities share.

title: Bloody Friday
summary: The IRA sets off around 20 bombs across Belfast in about 80 minutes. Nine people are killed, including two soldiers, and about 130 injured. Many of the warnings were confused or too late.
significance: A public relations disaster for the IRA, and it gave London the political cover to retake the no-go areas.

title: Operation Motorman ends Free Derry
summary: At dawn, thousands of troops with armoured bulldozers clear the barricades in Derry and Belfast. It is the largest British military operation since the 1956 Suez crisis.
significance: The end of the republican no-go areas. The IRA shifts to smaller cells and car bombs.

title: Claudy bombing
summary: Hours after Motorman, three car bombs explode in the village of Claudy, killing nine people, Catholic and Protestant. The IRA never admitted it. A 2010 police ombudsman report found a local priest suspected of involvement was moved across the border instead of being investigated.
significance: One of the clearest cases of the state, the Church and the IRA all failing victims.

title: Sunningdale Agreement
summary: The British and Irish governments and the moderate Northern parties agree a power-sharing executive of unionists and nationalists, plus a cross-border Council of Ireland.
significance: Nationalist SDLP politician Seamus Mallon later called the 1998 deal 'Sunningdale for slow learners'.
questions: Why did Sunningdale fail when the Good Friday Agreement didn't?

title: Dublin and Monaghan bombings
summary: Three UVF car bombs explode in Dublin's evening rush hour and a fourth in Monaghan 90 minutes later. Thirty-three people and an unborn child are killed. No one has ever been charged.
significance: The deadliest day of the Troubles. Allegations of collusion by British security forces have never been resolved.

title: Loyalist strike topples power-sharing
summary: The Ulster Workers' Council general strike, enforced by loyalist roadblocks, shuts down power stations and much of the economy. After two weeks the unionist ministers resign and the power-sharing executive collapses.
significance: Proved unionists could veto a settlement. Direct rule returns for the next 25 years.

title: Birmingham pub bombings
summary: IRA bombs in two city-centre pubs kill 21 people. Six Irishmen are convicted. The 'Birmingham Six' are freed in 1991, one of Britain's worst miscarriages of justice.
significance: Within days Parliament passes the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The IRA's campaign in Britain becomes a defining part of the Troubles.

title: Miami Showband killings
summary: UVF members, some also serving soldiers in the Ulster Defence Regiment, stop the popular band's minibus at a fake army checkpoint. A bomb they are hiding in the van explodes early, killing two of them. They then shoot dead three band members.
significance: A notorious case of collusion between loyalist paramilitaries and members of the security forces.

title: Maguire children killed; Peace People founded
summary: Soldiers shoot the driver of an IRA getaway car, which crashes into the Maguire family and kills three children. Their aunt Mairead Corrigan and local woman Betty Williams start the Peace People. Tens of thousands join their rallies.
significance: Corrigan and Williams receive the Nobel Peace Prize for 1976. The movement faded, but showed a huge appetite for peace on both sides.

title: Blanket protest begins
summary: Kieran Nugent, the first IRA prisoner denied 'special category' political status, refuses to wear a prison uniform and wraps himself in a blanket. Hundreds follow. By 1978 it escalates into the 'dirty protest'.
significance: Britain's criminalisation policy turned the prisons into the main battlefield of the late 1970s.

title: Lord Mountbatten killed
summary: An IRA bomb destroys Lord Mountbatten's fishing boat off Mullaghmore. Mountbatten, the Queen's cousin, is killed along with his teenage grandson, a 15-year-old local boy and an elderly relative.
significance: The same afternoon, the IRA attacked soldiers at Warrenpoint. It was one of the worst days of the conflict for the British establishment.
wiki: Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma

title: Warrenpoint ambush
summary: Two IRA bombs, the second aimed at the soldiers who rushed to help after the first, kill 18 British soldiers on the road beside Carlingford Lough.
significance: The British Army's biggest single loss of life in the Troubles.

title: Hunger striker Bobby Sands elected MP
summary: Forty days into his hunger strike for political status, IRA prisoner Bobby Sands wins the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election with 30,492 votes.
significance: Showed republicans that elections could be won. The seed of Sinn Féin's later political strategy.
questions: What were the hunger strikers' five demands?

title: Bobby Sands dies
summary: Sands dies on the 66th day of his hunger strike. Around 100,000 people attend his funeral. Nine more hunger strikers die before the strike ends on 3 October.
significance: Margaret Thatcher refused to give in, but the strikes were a huge propaganda win for republicans and set Sinn Féin on the road into electoral politics.
questions: Why did Thatcher refuse to give political status?

title: Droppin Well bombing
summary: An INLA bomb at a disco near an army base kills 11 soldiers and six civilians.
significance: The deadliest attack by the INLA, a smaller and more chaotic republican group than the IRA.

title: The Great Escape from the Maze
summary: Thirty-eight IRA prisoners hijack a food lorry and break out of the most secure prison in Europe. A prison officer dies of a heart attack after being stabbed.
significance: The biggest jailbreak in UK history, and a huge embarrassment for the government.

title: Brighton hotel bombing
summary: An IRA bomb planted weeks earlier explodes in the Grand Hotel during the Conservative Party conference. Margaret Thatcher escapes; five people are killed.
significance: The IRA's statement warned the government it only had to be lucky once. Thatcher opened the conference on time the next morning.

title: Anglo-Irish Agreement
summary: Margaret Thatcher and Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald give Dublin a formal advisory role in Northern Ireland affairs. Unionists are furious and hold a vast 'Ulster Says No' rally at Belfast City Hall.
significance: Unionists were not consulted and could not stop it. It locked London and Dublin together, the foundation of the later peace process.

title: Enniskillen Remembrance Day bombing
summary: An IRA bomb at the town's Remembrance Sunday service kills 11 people; a twelfth dies after 13 years in a coma. Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie died holding his hand under the rubble, says on BBC radio that he bears the bombers no ill will.
significance: Wilson's words became one of the most powerful moments of the Troubles, and the attack badly damaged the IRA's support.

title: Milltown Cemetery attack
summary: At the funeral of three IRA members shot by the SAS in Gibraltar, loyalist Michael Stone attacks mourners with grenades and a pistol, killing three. Three days later, two British Army corporals who drive into another funeral are dragged out and killed.
significance: Two weeks of televised horror that sum up the cycle of killing and funerals in the late 1980s.

title: Shankill bombing and Greysteel
summary: An IRA bomb meant for loyalist leaders goes off early in a crowded fish shop, killing nine civilians and one of the bombers. A week later, UFF gunmen shout 'trick or treat' and kill eight people in the Rising Sun bar in Greysteel.
significance: October 1993 was the bloodiest month in years, and it came as secret peace talks were already under way.

title: Downing Street Declaration
summary: John Major and Albert Reynolds declare that the people of Ireland alone can decide on unity, with the consent of a majority in the North, and that parties linked to paramilitaries can join talks if violence ends.
significance: Set out the principle of consent that sits at the heart of the 1998 deal.

title: IRA ceasefire
summary: The IRA announces 'a complete cessation of military operations'. Cars drive through west Belfast with horns blaring. Loyalist paramilitaries follow with their own ceasefire on 13 October.
significance: Deaths fell from 64 in 1994 to 9 in 1995.
questions: Why did the IRA call a ceasefire in 1994?

title: Canary Wharf bomb ends ceasefire
summary: Frustrated by the slow pace of talks, the IRA ends its 17-month ceasefire with a huge truck bomb in London's Docklands. Two men are killed.
significance: Showed the peace was fragile and the IRA could still hit the heart of the British economy.

title: Manchester bombing
summary: The IRA explodes the largest bomb in Britain since the Second World War in Manchester's shopping centre on a Saturday. Around 200 people are injured but no one is killed.
significance: The rebuilding of Manchester's centre became a story of its own.

title: IRA ceasefire restored
summary: After Tony Blair's landslide election, the IRA reinstates its ceasefire. Sinn Féin enters all-party talks chaired by US Senator George Mitchell that September.
significance: For the first time, everyone who mattered, except the DUP, was at the table.

title: Good Friday Agreement
summary: After an all-night session, the two governments and most parties agree a deal: a power-sharing Assembly, North–South bodies, Ireland drops its constitutional claim to the North, and paramilitary prisoners are released within two years. The DUP opposes it.
significance: Northern Ireland stays in the UK for as long as a majority wants that, and people can be British, Irish or both. It still underpins politics today.
questions: What did each side give up?
How does the principle of consent work?

title: Referendums North and South
summary: Voters approve the Agreement on the same day on both sides of the border: 71% yes in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic.
significance: The first all-Ireland vote since 1918, giving the deal a democratic mandate on the whole island.
wiki: 1998 Northern Ireland Good Friday Agreement referendum

title: Omagh bombing
summary: A Real IRA car bomb in Omagh's busy shopping street on a Saturday afternoon kills 29 people, including a woman pregnant with twins. Confused warnings led police to move people towards the bomb.
significance: The deadliest single attack of the Troubles in Northern Ireland. Revulsion across every community helped secure the peace instead of wrecking it.
